title: Startups average two or three people, running on the kitchen table
dek: a16z's Speedrun invests in "little tech": teams of two or three on average, running on the kitchen table, with no lobbyists and no time to join the rules discussion — and they are exactly the ones most easily hurt by rules.
why: Medium information density, but Andrew Chen gives the real granularity of early startups: team size, daily rhythm, where founders go after failure, and how regulation affects where they locate.
who: For early-stage investors, founders currently at the two-or-three-person stage, and anyone interested in how tech regulation affects where startups locate.
skip: The last two minutes of host thanks and disclaimers can be skipped.

points.h: Average two or three people, running on the kitchen table
points.body: Andrew Chen says what Speedrun invests in is "little tech" — teams of two to three on average, who are not running the company in an office or a co-working space, but on the kitchen table. This is the real source of a lot of American industrial success. On the upper bound, once a team goes past three, four, five people, you have to worry about equity getting split too thin, and some people need to actually draw a salary, so you rarely see teams bigger than that.

points.h: Not waiting for founders to show up, but helping build the company
points.body: Andrew Chen says that in his first few years at a16z he did Series A and Series B, writing $10 million, $15 million, $20 million checks, when the company already had customers, metrics, and a team. But what excites him about Speedrun is: not waiting for founders to show up at a16z's door, but helping create the company. The last Speedrun batch had 70 companies, and roughly a dozen of their founders still had full-time jobs at the time, had to hand back their laptops and badges, and in some cases could not be funded because they had not yet incorporated.

points.h: Co-founders live together 24-7 and do only two things
points.body: Andrew Chen describes the daily life of a Speedrun company: two founders fly in to San Francisco from Austin, Chicago, and elsewhere, and during the program usually room with their co-founder, together 24-7. The housing is not luxurious, generally near the a16z office, and they can walk, take an Uber, or ride a Waymo to the office. The only thing they should spend time on is figuring out whether this business can work — build the product, sell the product, and do it in a very short amount of time. Usually one more business-oriented co-founder handles meeting customers and negotiating deals, and one more technical and product-oriented co-founder uses AI coding heavily.

points.h: Half the companies just die, all the money is made in the top tenth
points.body: Andrew Chen says that in the venture capital industry, the colloquial description is that about half the companies cannot make it at all and just die; of the remaining five to ten, two or three make a little money; all the money is made in the top tenth, the one company that hits a home run. This math has been very consistent for decades. As for the ones that die, he thinks a lot of good things happen: a16z will invest in those founders again, and just last week it funded a founder with a better idea than the first one; some people need to recharge, rebuild their finances, focus on their health, and then get hired by other teams, and two or three years later come out with a new idea and start again.

points.h: Founders see regulation as friction, not an incremental burden
points.body: Matt Perault mentions that a16z wrote a piece called Greens from a Garage, about the regulatory landscape two people face when building the next great tool in a garage. He says policy teams often only count the "incremental burden" — what happens if you pass a new law; but the real picture is the stacking of all regulations: California's SB 53, the data provenance requirements from the last session, the privacy law passed a few years ago, all of which you have to comply with from the moment you start building the tool. Andrew Chen says that for founders, these obstacles just add friction, and many laws and paperwork are designed for companies much bigger than them, companies that have legal teams and expert teams to handle compliance.

points.h: They have no lobbyists and no time to shower
points.body: Andrew Chen says many founders simply have no time to participate: they have no lobbyists, they do not take part in the political process, and in many ways they are unrepresented, because they just do not have the time — they may not even have time to shower or eat a proper dinner, let alone do anything beyond daily survival. Matt Perault adds that this creates a compounding effect: a16z shows up to represent little tech, but it is not itself a founder, and people will say they would rather talk to a startup; but the startup is in a 100-hour work week and will not drive to Sacramento, fly to Washington, or fly to Brussels. The result is that what policymakers hear is a skewed perspective: they do not hear little tech, but they hear a lot from big tech and from disrupted industries.

points.h: Companies can choose where to put down roots, one of the most important choices
points.body: Andrew Chen says these teams are small and at the starting point, so they can choose where to start the company. When he moved to the Bay Area in 2007, the world still revolved around Palo Alto, Mountain View, and the Peninsula; later the center of the startup ecosystem moved as a whole from the Peninsula to downtown San Francisco, and later New York became a huge startup center, and major VCs also opened offices in London and across Europe. If from day one you know that building an AI company will come with a pile of extra rules, a two-or-three-person startup is very mobile and can pick a place. He mentions one data point: close to 50% of venture-backed startups are founded by first-generation immigrants. The Bay Area benefits from this, but that is not guaranteed to last forever.

points.h: Whether to have startups is a choice for every state and city
points.body: Asked what he would say to policymakers, Andrew Chen gives three points. First, whether every state and every city wants startups is a choice; if they want them, they have to do the things that let startups grow, and not just for founders, but also for angel investors, employees, and everyone around them. Second, many policymakers have not really talked to little tech, and that takes a bit more time, but they need to figure out what obstacles can be removed for these companies, and those obstacles are dynamic: software companies, AI-native companies, hardware companies, and robotics companies all say different things, and this year there are clearly more robotics companies than in past years, with different needs like supply chains and real estate. Third, a16z can help open the door to the conversation.

For us, one of the really magical things, something that I take a lot of just personal pride and excitement in, is the idea that we are not just waiting for entrepreneurs to show up at our doorstep at A16Z. But we're actually helping create the companies in the first place.
